catalog_quote: 6.2 Word Stress. Word stress in Sursurunga is predictable and operates according to the following rules: 1. When all syllables in the word are identical in both CV pattern and phoneme quality, stress tends to be equal on all syllables. 2. In all other cases, primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable with secondary stress on the alternate regressive syllables when they are present. Identical syllables: /'dik'dik'dik/ 'shaking', /'dok'dok/ 'fruit harvesting stick' ... 2-syllable words: /'guai/ 'to make wet', ... /'kalau/ 'male'. 3-syllable words: /gur'guran/ 'to wash clothes', /i'lilim/ 'to wash hands' ... 4-syllable words: /'alek'tadai/ 'to turn upside down', /'kalas'tari/ 'caught', /'kawa'liklik/ 'kinship group'. 5-syllable words: /u'tungti'mani/ 'to explain', /par'asak'saknai/ 'to relate untruthfully but not necessarily intentionally'.

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated locator (1985 Updated Phonology sec. 6.2, pp.17-18), verified from page images since the PDF has no text layer. The source is the most recent and most specific stress description that exists for Sursurunga, written by the long-term fieldworkers and explicitly superseding their weight/segment-driven 1975 'not yet fully analyzed' account (which our record correctly notes as superseded and which explains the 31 Aug quick-screen 'weight-sensitive' misclassification). The later 2018 dictionary (held, checked) is silent on stress, so nothing newer contradicts penultimate primary + alternating leftward secondary. Coding 'fixed penult, weight-blind, listed exception for fully identical-syllable words' matches the source exactly. One minor caveat worth keeping in mind, not an action: the typescript marks primary and secondary stress with the same r
